specPoints.text: know that the activity of a radioactive source decreases over a period of time and is measured in becquerels

primer.text: A radioactive source is measured by its activity — how many unstable nuclei decay each second, counted in becquerels. Every decay thins the ranks of remaining nuclei, so activity inevitably falls with time, while random flicker in the count rate betrays the process.

lessons.title: Activity and the becquerel
lessons.opening: The activity of a source is the rate at which its unstable nuclei decay, measured in becquerels: one becquerel means one decay per second. Objects carrying radioactive nuclei are sources, and different sources decay at different rates.
keyPoints: A source is an object containing radioactive nuclei.
Activity measures the rate at which unstable nuclei in the source decay.
One becquerel equals one nucleus decaying per second.
Different sources decay at different rates.

low.restatement: A 500 Bq source decays 500 nuclei every second; a 50 Bq source only 50. The unit counts decays, not particles seen.
low.analogy: Activity is popcorn pace — kernels popping per second — not the size of the pan.
low.examPointer: Quote the definition as a rate ("per second") — defining activity as just "how radioactive" earns nothing.

medium.restatement: Because each decay consumes one unstable nucleus, the population of decaying nuclei is strictly decreasing, so activity must decline over time — the law that half-life quantifies. The becquerel is small, so real sources quote kilo- or mega-becquerels.
medium.analogy: A candle burns its wax as it shines: the flame (activity) must eventually gutter because the fuel (unstable nuclei) is finite.
medium.examPointer: Keep activity (nuclei decaying) distinct from count rate (detections recorded) — examiners separate them deliberately.

check.stem: What is the activity of a radioactive source?

options.text: the rate at which its unstable nuclei decay
options.explanation: Activity is decays per unit time.

options.text: the number of nuclei it contains
options.explanation: That is a population, not a rate.

options.text: the energy of its emissions
options.explanation: Energy per emission is a different property.

options.text: the time it takes to become safe
options.explanation: That relates to half-life, not the definition.

options.text: one nucleus decaying per second
options.explanation: The Bq is a per-second decay rate.

options.text: one nucleus decaying per hour
options.explanation: The unit is per second.

options.text: one particle detected by a GM tube
options.explanation: Detections define count rate, not the becquerel.

options.text: one gram of radioactive material
options.explanation: Mass is not the unit of activity.

check.stem: Why must the activity of any source decrease with time?

options.text: because every decay removes one unstable nucleus from the source
options.explanation: The decaying population only shrinks.

options.text: because nuclei get heavier as they decay
options.explanation: Decay changes identity; the reasoning is about counts.

options.text: because detectors tire out
options.explanation: Detector behaviour does not alter the source.

options.text: because radiation damages the container
options.explanation: Container damage is irrelevant.

check.stem: A source has an activity of 8000 Bq. How many unstable nuclei decay in it each second?

options.explanation: 8000 Bq means 8000 decays per second.
The per-minute figure is not the activity quoted.
That inverts the rate.

options.text: it cannot be said from the activity
options.explanation: The definition answers directly.

check.stem: Which statement distinguishes activity from count rate?

options.text: activity counts decays in the source; count rate counts detections at the detector
options.explanation: The two live at opposite ends of the journey.

options.text: activity is measured in counts per minute
options.explanation: Activity is in becquerels.

options.text: count rate is always larger than activity
options.explanation: No fixed ordering exists.

options.text: they are two names for the same quantity
options.explanation: They are deliberately distinguished.

check.stem: Define the activity of a radioactive source.
check.modelAnswer: Activity measures the rate at which a source’s unstable nuclei decay.

check.stem: State the unit of activity and what one unit equals.
check.modelAnswer: Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq); one becquerel is one nucleus decaying per second.

check.stem: Explain why a source whose activity is 2000 Bq today must have a smaller activity in a year’s time.
check.modelAnswer: Each decay removes one unstable nucleus, so the number available to decay keeps falling; a smaller decaying population means a lower rate, hence a lower activity.

check.stem: A source’s activity is 400 Bq. How many unstable nuclei decay in 30 seconds, assuming the activity stays steady over that short window?

lessons.title: Activity falls, randomness shows
sourceHeadings: How does activity vary with time?
lessons.opening: Plot a source’s count rate against time and the trace slopes downward — each decay shrinks the pool of unstable nuclei — but the line wobbles, because decay is random. Those fluctuations are the experimental evidence for randomness itself.
keyPoints: The activity of a source decreases with time.
Each decay event reduces the number of radioactive nuclei left in the source.
Radioactive decay is a random process.
Count-rate fluctuations plotted against time are evidence for that randomness.

low.restatement: The graph trends down but zig-zags on the way: one minute high, next minute low, always drifting downward.
low.analogy: It is like rain drying on a window — the overall trend is fewer droplets, but which drop goes next is anyone’s guess.
low.examPointer: If asked for evidence of randomness, answer: the fluctuating count rate at constant conditions.

medium.restatement: The downward trend reflects the shrinking population of unstable nuclei; the scatter reflects independent, unpredictable decay events whose statistical noise never fully averages out over short windows. Distinguishing trend from noise is the graph-reading skill this topic tests.
medium.analogy: A popcorn pan rattles irregularly (random pops) while the popping rate overall falls as kernels run out (trend).
medium.examPointer: Quote both halves: decreasing overall, fluctuating locally. A smooth line answer misses the randomness mark.

check.stem: What does a falling count-rate trace indicate over time?

options.text: the source’s activity is decreasing
options.explanation: Fewer decays per second as nuclei run down.

options.text: the GM tube is failing
options.explanation: The trend is physical, not instrumental.

options.text: the source is absorbing radiation
options.explanation: Sources emit; they do not absorb into inactivity.

options.text: background radiation is rising
options.explanation: Background is steady; the trend is the source’s.

check.stem: What do the fluctuations on a count-time graph demonstrate?

options.text: that radioactive decay is a random process
options.explanation: Irregular wobble at fixed conditions is the randomness evidence.

options.text: that the GM tube is faulty
options.explanation: Fluctuation is expected physics, not fault.

options.text: that activity increases with time
options.explanation: The trend is downward.

options.text: that the source is contaminated
options.explanation: No contamination is needed to explain the wobble.

check.stem: Why does each decay event make the source slightly less active?

options.text: one fewer unstable nucleus remains to decay later
options.explanation: The decaying population shrinks one nucleus at a time.

options.text: the emitted radiation removes energy from the source
options.explanation: Energy loss is not the population argument.

options.text: the detector counts fewer because it moves away
options.explanation: Geometry is unrelated here.

options.text: the nuclei get too heavy to decay
options.explanation: Weight is not the mechanism.

check.stem: A corrected count rate at fixed geometry reads 41, 38, 43, 39 over four minutes. The best interpretation is…

options.text: a roughly steady activity with random fluctuation
options.explanation: Scatter about a level is the random signature.

options.text: the activity is doubling each minute
options.explanation: The readings hover, they do not double.

options.text: the detector is broken
options.explanation: Scatter is normal.

options.text: background was subtracted twice
options.explanation: Nothing suggests a subtraction error.

check.stem: Which graph sketch matches a decaying source’s count rate against time?

options.text: a downward-sloping, wobbly curve
options.explanation: Decreasing overall with random fluctuation.

options.text: a straight horizontal line
options.explanation: That would mean constant activity.

options.text: a smooth upward curve
options.explanation: Activity cannot rise in an isolated source.

options.text: a perfectly smooth exponential only
options.explanation: The randomness forbids perfect smoothness at the count level.

check.stem: State what happens to the activity of a source over time, and why.
check.modelAnswer: The activity decreases over time because each decay event reduces the number of unstable nuclei remaining in the source.

check.stem: Name the graph feature cited as evidence for the randomness of decay.
check.modelAnswer: The fluctuations of the count rate plotted against time are cited as evidence of randomness.

check.stem: Explain why the count rate of a steady-geometry source still wobbles from minute to minute.
check.modelAnswer: Decay is random: which nucleus decays in any second is unpredictable, so the number of emissions per interval fluctuates around the average set by the activity.

check.stem: A teacher shows two traces: one perfectly smooth and falling, one wobbly and falling. Which better represents a real corrected count rate, and why?
check.modelAnswer: The wobbly falling trace: real decay is random, so counts fluctuate while the overall downward trend from the shrinking unstable population persists.

glossary.definition: The rate at which unstable nuclei in a source decay.
The unit of activity: one decay per second.
The number of radiation detections per unit time at the detector.
An object containing radioactive nuclei that emits radiation.

workedExample.prompt: A source has an activity of 2000 Bq. How many unstable nuclei decay in 2 minutes?
steps: 2000 Bq means 2000 nuclei decay every second.
